Measures of central tendency
(Arithmetic) Mean: Also known as the average, is the sum of the
values divided by the number of values
• Median: The middle value that separates a data set into a
higher and a lower half
• Mode: It is the value that appears more frequently in a data set
(Arithmetic) Mean: Also known as the average, is the sum of the
values divided by the number of values
• Median: The middle value that separates a data set into a
higher and a lower half
• Mode: It is the value that appears more frequently in a data set

Median
The median of a data set is the value in the middle when the data items
are arranged in ascending order.
▪ Whenever a data set has extreme values, the median is the preferred
measure of central location.
Not always
▪ The median is the measure of location most often ( )
reported for annual income and property value data.
▪ A few extremely large incomes or property values can inflate the mean.

slides.text:
Mode
The mode of a data set is the value that occurs with the greatest
frequency.
▪ The greatest frequency can occur at two or more different values.
▪ If the data have exactly two modes, the data are bimodal.
▪ If the data have more than two modes, the data are multimodal.

slides.title: Which Measure to Use?
slides.text: Which Measure to Use?
slides.visual_text: A table titled Which Measure to Use? with columns Measures of Central Tendency, Pros and Cons. Mean: pros, takes all the values into account, sensitive and reliable; cons, biased in presence of extreme values. Median: pros, not effected by extreme values; cons, less sensitive than mean. Mode (only way to represent Nominal data): pros, not effected by extreme values and can be used for qualitative data; cons, it can take multiple values or no value at all, less sensitive than mean.

slides.visual_text: Left, For ungrouped data (Raw): Q1 = ((n + 1)/4)th term; Q2 = ((n + 1)/2)th term (Median); Q3 = (3(n + 1)/4)th term. Right, For grouped data (Class Intervals): Qk = L + ((k · n/4 - F)/f) · h, where Qk is the k-th quartile (k = 1, 2, 3), L is the lower boundary of the quartile class, n is the total frequency, F is the cumulative frequency before the quartile class, f is the frequency of the quartile class, and h is the width of the class interval. Bottom: Interquartile Range (IQR) = Q3 - Q1, with Purpose of IQR: measures the spread of the middle 50% of the data; useful for identifying outliers and understanding data variability; less affected by extreme values than the range.

Percentile Computation
Arrange the data in ascending order.
Compute index i , the position of the pth percentile.
i=(p/100) *n
If i is not an integer, round up. The pth percentile is the value in I th
position.
If i is an integer. The pth percentile is the average value in i th and i+1 th

of dollars, in no particular order, is as follows: 33, 26, 24, 21, 19, 20, 18,
18, 52, 56, 27, 22, 18, 49, 22, 20, 23, 32, 20, 18 Find the 50th and 80th
percentiles of this set of the world’s top 20 net worth’s

22, 22, 23, 24, 26, 27, 32, 33, 49, 52, 56
Step 2: Compute the Index using the formula: i = (p/100)n

Stores consistently below the average monthly sales per store may need support or a revised strategy; identify those stores. 2. If several stores cluster at a particular figure, investigate what common feature these stores have (location, management style, product mix) to replicate success elsewhere; identify the cluster of such stores. 3. Divide the stores into four equal groups based on sales; stores in the lowest quartile (Q1) might need urgent intervention or training, top quartile (Q4) performers can be studied for best practices. 4. Create special rewards for stores that break into the top 10% to get performance incentives; identify the stores for this reward.
